#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail the build if VERSION, the Go const, and package.json disagree."""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]


def main() -> int:
    version = (ROOT / "VERSION").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()

    go = (ROOT / "internal" / "version" / "version.go").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    go_match = re.search(r'const Version = "([^"]+)"', go)
    package = json.loads((ROOT / "packages" / "npm" / "package.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    found = {
        "VERSION": version,
        "internal/version/version.go": go_match.group(1) if go_match else "missing",
        "packages/npm/package.json": package["version"],
    }

    if len(set(found.values())) == 1:
        print(f"Version sync OK: {version}")
        return 0

    print("Version mismatch:", file=sys.stderr)
    for where, value in found.items():
        flag = " " if value == version else "<-"
        print(f"  {flag} {where}: {value}", file=sys.stderr)
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

name: SecSentry
description: Scan this repo for leaked secrets (working tree + git history). Posts a PR check like other GitHub Apps.
author: SecSentry
branding:
  icon: shield
  color: gray-dark

inputs:
  path:
    description: Repository path to scan
    required: false
    default: "."
  history:
    description: Scan full git history (needs fetch-depth 0)
    required: false
    default: "true"
  fail-on:
    description: Fail the check at this severity (low, medium, high, critical)
    required: false
    default: "high"
  comment:
    description: Comment a masked summary on pull requests
    required: false
    default: "true"

outputs:
  findings-count:
    description: Number of findings at or above fail-on
    value: ${{ steps.scan.outputs.findings-count }}
  report-path:
    description: JSON report path
    value: ${{ steps.scan.outputs.report-path }}

runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Set up Go
      uses: actions/setup-go@v5
      with:
        go-version: "1.22"

    - name: Build SecSentry
      shell: bash
      run: go build -o "${RUNNER_TEMP}/secsentry" "${{ github.action_path }}/cmd/secsentry"

    - name: Scan
      id: scan
      shell: bash
      env:
        FAIL_ON: ${{ inputs.fail-on }}
        HISTORY: ${{ inputs.history }}
        SCAN_PATH: ${{ inputs.path }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        ARGS=(scan "$SCAN_PATH" --format json --fail-on "$FAIL_ON")
        if [ "$HISTORY" = "true" ]; then
          ARGS+=(--history)
        fi
        mkdir -p .secsentry
        REPORT=".secsentry/github-action.json"
        set +e
        "${RUNNER_TEMP}/secsentry" "${ARGS[@]}" --output "$REPORT"
        STATUS=$?
        set -e
        COUNT=0
        if [ -f "$REPORT" ]; then
          COUNT=$(jq '.findings | length' "$REPORT")
        fi
        echo "findings-count=$COUNT" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
        echo "report-path=$REPORT" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
        echo "## SecSentry" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
        echo "Findings: **$COUNT** (fail-on: \`$FAIL_ON\`, history: \`$HISTORY\`)" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
        echo >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
        echo "Secrets are masked. This check never sends keys to vendor APIs." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
        if [ "$COUNT" -gt 0 ] && [ -f "$REPORT" ]; then
          jq -r '
            "",
            "| Severity | Type | File | Line | Why |",
            "|---|---|---|---|---|",
            (.findings[:40][] | "| \(.severity) | \(.secret_type) | `\(.path)` | \(.line) | \((.why // []) | join("; ") | .[0:80]) |")
          ' "$REPORT" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
        fi
        exit "$STATUS"

    - name: Comment on pull request
      if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && inputs.comment == 'true' }}
      uses: actions/github-script@v7
      with:
        script: |
          const fs = require('fs');
          const path = '.secsentry/github-action.json';
          let count = 0;
          let body = '## SecSentry\n\nNo JSON report produced.';
          if (fs.existsSync(path)) {
            const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(path, 'utf8'));
            const findings = data.findings || [];
            count = findings.length;
            const rows = findings.slice(0, 20).map(f =>
              `| ${f.severity || ''} | ${f.secret_type || ''} | \`${f.path || ''}\` | ${f.line || ''} | \`${f.masked || ''}\` |`
            );
            body = [
              '## SecSentry secret scan',
              '',
              count ? `**${count}** finding(s). Values are masked; file and line are shown so you can rotate. Anything HIGH/CRITICAL should be treated as leaked.` : 'No findings at the configured severity.',
              '',
              count ? '| Severity | Type | File | Line | Masked |' : '',
              count ? '|---|---|---|---|---|' : '',
              ...rows,
              '',
              '_This check does not send secrets to OpenAI, AWS, or GitHub APIs._',
            ].filter(Boolean).join('\n');
          }
          const { data: comments } = await github.rest.issues.listComments({
            owner: context.repo.owner,
            repo: context.repo.repo,
            issue_number: context.issue.number,
          });
          const marker = '## SecSentry secret scan';
          const existing = comments.find(c => c.user.type === 'Bot' && c.body.includes(marker));
          if (existing) {
            await github.rest.issues.updateComment({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              comment_id: existing.id,
              body,
            });
          } else {
            await github.rest.issues.createComment({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              body,
            });
          }

# ADR-008 One engine, Go binary

## Context

v1 shipped a Python engine and an npm wrapper that spawned it. Converting the product to Go means we must not keep two detector implementations. Duplicating rules in Python and Go would drift and double the false-positive work.

## Decision

- The **Go module** (`github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry`) is the engine and the CLI
- Install path is `go install github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry/cmd/secsentry@latest`

- The GitHub Action builds the Go binary with `setup-go`

## Consequences

- Node users need the Go binary on PATH (document clearly in the npm README)
- One test suite (`go test ./...`) covers detection
- The older Python tree is not the product engine

# Prowl (Lercas/prowl)

Read 2026-09-04 from the public README. [github.com/Lercas/prowl](https://github.com/Lercas/prowl). **27 stars**, Go, PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0.

Prowl is the scanner that already occupies the “high-recall Go CLI, mask by default, SARIF, git history, archives” slot. It is not a Gitleaks clone and it is not zerosecret. Treat it as the **closest shipped product**, not as something to out-F1 on ProwlBench.

## What it is

A cascade:

1. **L1** — regex + keyword (Aho-Corasick) + checksum (Luhn, GitHub CRC, JWT) + Shannon entropy. Ships in every binary.
2. **L2** — optional `--ml` HistGradientBoosting over 49 features, or `--ml-url` sidecar. Static Homebrew/Docker builds **refuse** in-process `--ml`.
3. **`--verify`** — call the vendor’s read-only identity API and report live/dead, plus “blast radius” probes (what the key unlocks).

Surfaces we do not have and are not racing: org-wide GitHub/GitLab, Jira/Confluence, container images, S3/GCS, APK/IPA, live `--authorized` domains, CI logs, MCP server, OCR, Office docs, 159 YAML rules, drop-in `.gitleaks.toml`.

It **masks by default**. `--show-secrets` unmasks for “authorized triage.” That is the opposite of [[ADR-004 Mask secrets never print them]] — we never offer an unmask flag.

Git: `--staged`, `--since <rev>` (diffs), `--history` (every blob). Grouped by **file**, not by fingerprint. README does not mention still-in-HEAD or introduced-by as first-class state.

## Their own benchmark, quoted honestly

ProwlBench: 24,603 cases (16,552 pos / 8,051 neg). Published leaderboard:

| Tool | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prowl** cascade | 0.951 | 0.823 | **0.883** |
| detect-secrets | 0.848 | 0.423 | 0.564 |
| gitleaks | 0.931 | 0.413 | 0.573 |
| deepsecrets | 0.921 | 0.309 | 0.462 |
| trufflehog | 0.940 | 0.303 | 0.458 |

**They say the quiet part:** 57% of positives are generic passwords in multilingual prose. Gitleaks and TruffleHog are not designed for that tier, so the recall gap **narrows on structured tokens**. On a second check against clean `psf/requests`, **gitleaks is quietest (4 findings)**; Prowl cascade 18, Prowl `--ml` 9. They do not claim to beat Gitleaks on real clean code.

We will not run ProwlBench and paste a SecSentry row. That corpus is their product. Our planted 25-secret table would look like their “set (A) is biased toward Prowl” footnote.

## License

**PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** — free for noncommercial use, not for commercial products. SecSentry is MIT. That is a real adoption difference, not a quality one.

## What to steal locally (no network)

- **PEM header alone is not a key.** They require a body. We now do too.
- Mask by default (we already do; they add an unmask flag we will not copy).
- Archives + decode (we already do).
- Keyword prefilter (we already do; they use Aho-Corasick because they have 159 rules).

## What not to steal

- `--verify` and capability probes. [[ADR-009 No live secret verification]]
- `--show-secrets`
- The 159-rule YAML library and gitleaks.toml compatibility as a v1 pitch
- Org / Jira / image / domain scanners
- Claiming ProwlBench F1

## How we still have a slice

Prowl answers “is there a credential in this blob / ticket / image?” SecSentry answers **“is this the same secret, who first committed it, and is it still in HEAD?”** Unique-secret aggregation, rotation text, and a localhost case-file dashboard are not in their README. Zero-exfil is a *guarantee* for us and an *optional off switch* for them.

If an examiner asks “why not just use Prowl?”: they should, if they want live verify, 159 rules, and Jira. Use SecSentry if they want an **incident file** that never leaves the box and can be shipped commercially under MIT.

Ran 2026-09-04 with the published [Lercas/prowlbench](https://github.com/Lercas/prowlbench) protocol on `Podric/prowl-secrets-corpus` (`prowlbench.parquet`). Snippet-level flag ≥ 1. Artifact: `eval/results/prowlbench_leaderboard.json`. Charts: the ProwlBench results canvas.

**Gitleaks and TruffleHog match the published leaderboard exactly** (F1 0.573 and 0.458). The harness is fair. Prowl cascade is quoted from their README, not re-run.

| Tool | Precision | Recall | F1 | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prowl cascade (published) | 0.951 | 0.823 | **0.883** | 0.853 |
| Gitleaks | 0.931 | 0.413 | 0.573 | 0.585 |
| **SecSentry 1.2.0** | **0.951** | 0.347 | 0.509 | 0.549 |
| TruffleHog | 0.940 | 0.303 | 0.458 | 0.518 |

Counts for this run: SecSentry TP 5748 / FP 298 / FN 10804 / TN 7753.

### Per-tier (T1–T3 = recall, T4 = FP rate)

| Tool | T1 structured (n=7033) | T2 generic-context (n=3519) | T3 free-form multilingual (n=6000) | T4 hard-negative FP (n=8051) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SecSentry** | 0.64 | **0.01** | 0.20 | **0.037** |
| Gitleaks | 0.65 | 0.35 | 0.17 | 0.063 |
| TruffleHog | 0.60 | 0.00 | 0.13 | 0.040 |

T1 is a dead heat with Gitleaks. T2 is the hole: we almost never fire on unlabeled generic keys/passwords; Gitleaks does. T4 we are the quietest of the three we ran.

### How to read this

Highest **precision** of the three tools we executed. We lose **recall** because the set is full of `generic_password` / prose keys we do not target (top misses: generic_password 3284, generic_api_key 3143, generic_high_entropy 1101). That is the same disclosure Prowl makes about 57% of the positives.

This number is allowed to mean: on an independent structured+prose corpus, we are a high-precision prefix scanner, not a multilingual password finder.

It is **not** allowed to mean we beat Prowl. Their cascade F1 is 0.883 on this set; we did not re-run their binary.

## Where the others are genuinely better

- **Prowl** — 159 rules, optional ML, Jira/images/org scan, live `--verify`, and the recall this corpus is built to reward. PolyForm Noncommercial. [[Prowl]]
- **Gitleaks** ships far more rules and wins T2 generic-context (0.35 vs our 0.01). On Prowl's clean-OSS check, Gitleaks is the quietest.
- **TruffleHog** can say "this key still logs in." We refuse ([[ADR-009 No live secret verification]]).
- **zerosecret** has SecretBench loaders. ProwlBench we have now run.

<timestamp>Friday, Sep 4, 2026, 1:35 AM (UTC-4)</timestamp>
<user_query>
how we can increase recall ?
</user_query>
The miss list in the ProwlBench artifact already shows where recall is leaking. I’ll map those gaps onto our detectors and rank what would actually move the number.

**Most of the 10,804 misses are types we chose not to hunt.** Closing them all would make us Prowl. Closing the *structured* ones would raise recall without wrecking precision.

Of 16,552 positives we caught 5,748 (recall **0.347**). The FN pile:

| Bucket | Misses | Share of FN | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generic_password` + `generic_api_key` + `generic_high_entropy` | 7,528 | **70%** | Unlabeled secrets in prose / assignments |
| Missing vendor prefixes | ~1,638 | 15% | Telegram, Discord, Slack webhook, Azure, Datadog, DigitalOcean |
| `basic_auth_header` | 613 | 6% | `Authorization: Basic …` |
| PEM / GCP JSON / Twilio / DB / AWS secret | ~891 | 8% | Rules we have, but too tight |

T1 (structured) is already **0.64 vs Gitleaks 0.65**. T2 is **0.01 vs 0.35**. That is the whole story.

### 1. Cheap, on-brand (do this)

Add prefix rules we simply do not have. Public token shapes, same as Square/Shopify:

- Slack incoming webhook `https://hooks.slack.com/services/T…/B…/…`
- Discord `MTxxxx.xxx.xxx` / bot tokens
- Telegram `123456:ABC…`
- Azure storage account keys
- Datadog `****` 32-hex
- DigitalOcean `dop_v1_…`

Optimistic ceiling if we catch ~80% of those 1,638: recall **0.35 → ~0.43**, which would **pass Gitleaks (0.413)** while keeping the high-precision story. T4 should barely move if the prefixes are specific.

Also loosen what we already have, carefully:

- **PEM:** we now require a body — that likely explains some of the 246 `private_key_pem` misses (snippet is header-only, or `BEGIN OPENSSH` already covered). Allow more PEM flavours (`ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY`, `EC PRIVATE KEY` as its own header).
- **GCP JSON:** require fewer fields so a truncated snippet still flags.
- **AWS secret:** also fire when the 40-char blob sits on the line *after* an `AKIA`/`ASIA` (paired), not only `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=`.
- **DB URLs:** `http://user:pass@` / `jdbc:mysql://` / SQLAlchemy forms; 160 misses.
- **Twilio:** `SK` we have; many cases are Account SID **plus** auth token, or `AC` we correctly ignore. Only add the 32-hex auth token when `TWILIO` / `AC` is nearby.

### 2. Medium, still on-brand

- **`basic_auth_header`:** `Authorization:\s*Basic\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{20,}` then decode and check `user:pass`. Real leaks, not prose.
- **Widen `generic_api_key`:** we only match `api_key = "…"`. ProwlBench T2 is `token:`, `password:`, YAML, JSON, `export FOO=`. Adding a few assignment shapes (`token`, `password`, `credential` + quoted 20+ charset) is how Gitleaks gets T2=0.35. **This is the precision risk.** Gate with entropy + BPE rarity or T4 will climb from 0.037 toward Gitleaks’ 0.063.

### 3. Do not do this to “win ProwlBench”

- **`generic_password` in German/French/Russian prose** (T3, 6,000 cases). That is Prowl’s ML. Recall 0.82 lives there. Copying it means a language model or a huge keyword list, and it fights ADR-009 / the incident-scanner pitch.
- Free-floating 40-char “AWS secrets” and unlabeled high-entropy. Zerosecret already showed that FP factory.

### What “good” looks like

| Goal | How | Expected recall (ballpark) |
|---|---|---|
| Beat Gitleaks on this set | Vendor prefixes + Basic auth + slightly wider assignments | **~0.42–0.45** |
| Stay highest precision | Keep unlabeled entropy off | T4 stays ~0.04 |
| Match Prowl 0.82 | Multilingual password ML | Out of scope |

The honest line for an examiner: **T1 is already Gitleaks. Recall is low because we refuse T2/T3 unlabeled secrets. The next 8 points of recall are six token prefixes, not a neural net.**

I can implement pack 1 (the six prefixes + PEM/GCP/AWS-secret pairing) in this repo if you want that next.

import json, re, collections
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("/Users/muhamamd/Documents/secsentry/eval/results/prowlbench_cases.jsonl")

discord_lens = collections.Counter()
telegram_lens = collections.Counter()
azure_lens = collections.Counter()
dop_pref = collections.Counter()
basic_lens = collections.Counter()
pem_headers = collections.Counter()
aws_secret_ctx = collections.Counter()
db_schemes = collections.Counter()
twilio_sk = 0
twilio_hex = 0
gcp_one_line = 0
gcp_has_email = 0
gcp_has_begin = 0
gcp_n = 0

re_disc = re.compile(r"\b([\w-]{20,30})\.([\w-]{5,8})\.([\w-]{20,50})\b")
re_tg = re.compile(r"\b(\d{6,12}):([A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,45})\b")
re_az = re.compile(r"AccountKey=([A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)", re.I)
re_dop = re.compile(r"\b(do[por]_v1_)[a-f0-9]+", re.I)
re_basic = re.compile(r"Authorization['\"\s:=]*Basic\s+['\"]?([A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)", re.I)
re_pem = re.compile(r"-----BEGIN ([A-Z ]+)-----")
re_jdbc = re.compile(r"jdbc:([a-z0-9]+):", re.I)

# We don't have labels in this jsonl. Heuristic counts on likely positives.
for line in p.open():
    c = json.loads(line)
    t = c["text"]
    for m in re_disc.finditer(t):
        discord_lens[(len(m.group(1)), len(m.group(2)), len(m.group(3)))] += 1
    for m in re_tg.finditer(t):
        telegram_lens[(len(m.group(1)), len(m.group(2)), m.group(2)[:2])] += 1
    for m in re_az.finditer(t):
        azure_lens[len(m.group(1))] += 1
    for m in re_dop.finditer(t):
        dop_pref[m.group(1).lower()] += 1
    for m in re_basic.finditer(t):
        basic_lens[len(m.group(1))] += 1
    for m in re_pem.finditer(t):
        pem_headers[m.group(1)] += 1
    if "service_account" in t:
        gcp_n += 1
        if "\n" not in t.strip() or t.count("\n") <= 1:
            gcp_one_line += 1
        if "iam.gserviceaccount.com" in t:
            gcp_has_email += 1
        if "BEGIN " in t and "PRIVATE KEY" in t:
            gcp_has_begin += 1
    if "twilio" in t.lower():
        if re.search(r"\bSK[0-9a-fA-F]{32}\b", t):
            twilio_sk += 1
        elif re.search(r"[0-9a-fA-F]{32}", t):
            twilio_hex += 1
    if re.search(r"(?i)secret_access_key", t):
        if re.search(r"(?i)secret_access_key\s*[:=]\s*['\"]?[A-Za-z0-9/+=]{40}", t):
            aws_secret_ctx["colon_eq_40"] += 1
        elif re.search(r"(?i)secret_access_key.{0,30}[A-Za-z0-9/+=]{40}", t):
            aws_secret_ctx["window_40"] += 1
        else:
            aws_secret_ctx["other"] += 1
    for m in re_jdbc.finditer(t):
        db_schemes[m.group(1).lower()] += 1

print("discord segment lens", discord_lens.most_common(10))
print("telegram (idlen, toklen, prefix)", telegram_lens.most_common(10))
print("azure AccountKey lens", azure_lens)
print("dop prefixes", dop_pref)
print("basic b64 lens", basic_lens.most_common(8))
print("pem headers", pem_headers)
print("gcp n", gcp_n, "oneline-ish", gcp_one_line, "email", gcp_has_email, "begin", gcp_has_begin)
print("twilio SK", twilio_sk, "hex32 no SK", twilio_hex)
print("aws secret ctx", aws_secret_ctx)
print("jdbc schemes", db_schemes)

import json, re, collections
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("/Users/muhamamd/Documents/secsentry/eval/results/prowlbench_cases.jsonl")

# schemes that look like URLs with user:pass@
re_url = re.compile(r"(?i)\b([a-z][a-z0-9+.-]{1,30})://[^\s'\"<>]+")
schemes = collections.Counter()
examples = collections.defaultdict(list)
# filter those with : and @ in the authority
for line in p.open():
    t = json.loads(line)["text"]
    for m in re_url.finditer(t):
        scheme = m.group(1).lower()
        url = m.group(0)
        if "@" in url and ":" in url.split("@",1)[0]:
            schemes[scheme] += 1
            if len(examples[scheme]) < 2:
                # redact password
                red = re.sub(r"://([^:]+):([^@]+)@", r"://\1:***@", url)[:120]
                examples[scheme].append(red)

print("user:pass@ schemes:")
for s,n in schemes.most_common(30):
    print(f"  {n:4d} {s}  e.g. {examples[s][0]}")

# connection strings that aren't URL-shaped
# sqlserver, odbc, etc
other = collections.Counter()
for line in p.open():
    t = json.loads(line)["text"]
    low = t.lower()
    if "server=" in low and "password=" in low:
        other["server+password"] += 1
    if "data source=" in low and "password=" in low:

    if "jdbc:" in low:

The product people install is the **Go module**, not PyPI and not GitHub Packages. Those PyPI tabs are leftover from the old Python engine. Do not upload `src/secsentry` to PyPI — that would ship a second, stale scanner.

There are no tags yet, which is why the Releases sidebar is empty. `VERSION` is already `1.3.0`.

**1. Make the repo public** (if anyone besides you should install it)

`go install github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry/cmd/secsentry@latest` only works on a public repo. While it stays private, only machines with GitHub auth can fetch the module.

**2. Tag and create the GitHub release**

From this repo, after `main` is what you want to ship:

```bash
git tag -a v1.3.0 -m "SecSentry 1.3.0"
git push origin v1.3.0

gh release create v1.3.0 --title "1.3.0" --notes-file CHANGELOG.md --verify-tag
```

That fills **Releases**. After the tag exists:

```bash
go install github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry/cmd/secsentry@v1.3.0
# or
go install github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry/cmd/secsentry@latest
```

The GitHub Action is then `umeraamir69/secsentry@v1.3.0`.

The tag must match `VERSION` exactly (`v1.3.0` ↔ `1.3.0`). The Release workflow checks that.

**3. npm is optional, and it is only a wrapper**

`packages/npm` does not contain the scanner. It runs the Go binary already on `PATH`. First publish has to be **manual** (npm cannot create a new package via OIDC):

```bash
cd packages/npm
npm publish --dry-run    # read the file list
npm publish --access public   # 2FA prompt
```

Then on npmjs.com → package settings → **Trusted Publisher**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| User | `umeraamir69` |
| Repository | `secsentry` |
| Workflow | `release.yml` |
| Environment | `npm` |

Later `v*` tags can publish npm from CI. You can skip npm entirely; Go install is the real distribution.

**4. Ignore “No packages published”**

That is GitHub’s own registry. You do not need it. Do not publish the Python tree.

---

Order that matches this repo: **public repo → tag `v1.3.0` → GitHub Release → `go install` → (optional) npm**. I can create the tag and release from here if you want that next.

We do **not** compete by copying Gitleaks’ 200 rules or Prowl’s live `--verify`. Those races are already lost, and they fight our product (mask always, no vendor HTTP, incident case file).

The real hole vs Gitleaks was **T2 labeled assignments** (their recall 0.35, ours 0.01). That is now **1.4.0** (commit `5540f3f`, not tagged yet).

**In 1.4.0**
- Unquoted `API_KEY=…` / `SECRET_KEY=…` when entropy is high (quoted-only was the miss)
- `PASSWORD=` / `passwd=` / `pwd=` with the same gate — still **not** “the password is hunter2” in a sentence
- xAI `xai-` and Perplexity `pplx-`
- GitHub Release **binaries** (linux/macOS/windows) via GoReleaser, so people are not stuck on `go install`

**Still not doing** (on purpose)
- Passwords in multilingual prose (ProwlBench’s 57%)
- Unlabeled high-entropy blobs
- Calling AWS/OpenAI to see if a key is live
- An unmask flag

That is how we stay in the slice Gitleaks/TruffleHog/Prowl do not own: **who introduced it, still in HEAD, rotate, never reprint the value.**

To publish 1.4.0 (npm/PyPI/binaries): push `main`, tag `v1.4.0`. Say if you want that next.

# SecSentry

A Git **incident** scanner for leaked secrets. It searches the working tree and the full commit history, deduplicates by blob so the same object is never scanned twice, and reports every finding as a case file: what leaked, where, who introduced it, whether it is still in HEAD, and how to revoke it.

Values are always masked. SecSentry never sends a credential to a vendor API to check whether it still works.

> **This PyPI package is a PATH wrapper.** The detectors live in the Go binary. `pip install secsentry` gives you the `secsentry` console script; that script still needs the Go CLI on `PATH`.

## Install

```bash
# 1. Engine (required)
go install github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry/cmd/secsentry@latest
# or download a binary from GitHub Releases: linux / macOS / Windows

# 2. This wrapper (optional — only if you want `pip` / `uv` on PATH)
```

        working-directory: packages/npm
        env:

        run: |

Security
SecSentry

A Git incident scanner for leaked secrets. It searches the working tree and the full commit history, deduplicates by blob so the same object is never scanned twice across branches, and reports every finding as a case file: what leaked, where, who introduced it, whether it is still in HEAD, and how to revoke it.

Values are always masked. SecSentry never sends a credential to a vendor API to check whether it still works.

go install github.com/umeraamir69/secsentry/cmd/secsentry@latest
# or download a binary from GitHub Releases (linux / macOS / windows)

secsentry scan .              # working tree
secsentry scan . --history    # every commit
secsentry serve .  --history  # dashboard on 127.0.0.1
pip install secsentry and npx secsentry are wrappers. They still need that Go binary on PATH.

The problem

You delete an API key from config.py, commit, and move on. The key is still in git log, still in every clone, and still valid. A scanner that only reads the working tree tells you everything is fine.

$ secsentry scan ~/code/app
0 unique secret(s)                       # the tree is clean

$ secsentry scan ~/code/app --history
8 unique secret(s), 11 occurrence(s)  —  2 critical  4 high  2 medium

[CRITICAL] aws_access_key  AKIA••••••••••••ZZZZ  confidence=0.90
    .env:2:19  3836986b
    app/config.py:4:22  3836986b
    introduced by Umer Aamir on 2026-09-04
    deleted from HEAD, still in history
    why: rule=aws_access_key; structural_ok; entropy=2.92
    fix: IAM → Users → Security credentials → deactivate, then delete this key.
Live demo repository: umeraamir69/testKeys — secrets committed, then deleted, and still fully recoverable.

What it does

Layer	Behaviour
Scanner	Working tree, staged diff, or full history. Each unique blob OID is read once. Decode (base64 / hex / percent) and archives (zip / tar / gz) so a key in echo KEY | base64 or deploy.zip!.env is still a case file.
Detectors	AWS, GitHub, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Stripe, Slack (bot + webhook), Discord, Telegram, Azure storage, Datadog, DigitalOcean, xAI, Perplexity, Groq, HuggingFace, Square, Shopify, SendGrid, Twilio, GitLab, npm, PyPI, private keys, JWTs, Basic auth, database URLs, labeled API_KEY= / PASSWORD= plus Shannon entropy.
Verification	Prefix, length, and format checks performed locally. No network calls, ever.
Classifier	Path heuristics, Shannon entropy, and a local BPE rarity score. No network, no vendor model.
Reporting	Terminal, JSON, SARIF, self-contained HTML, and a localhost dashboard. Masked everywhere.
Enforcement	Pre-commit hook and a GitHub Action that fails the build and comments on the PR.
Masking hides the value, not the location

You cannot rotate what you cannot find, so every report shows path:line:column, the commit, and the author. What it never shows is a pasteable credential. Duplicates are tracked by SHA-256 fingerprint, and the allowlist accepts fingerprints — never raw secrets.

Benchmark

Two measurements. The first is the incident we actually sell. The second is a regression corpus — read it skeptically.

Demo: deleted keys still in git (testKeys)

Working tree is clean. History is not.

Tool	Findings	Case file	Raw secret in output
SecSentry 1.2.0	8 unique / 11 occ, all still_in_head=false	who / when / rotate	no
zerosecret	9 occurrences, not aggregated	no	yes (matched_string)
Gitleaks 8.30	7 (missed the AWS key)	commit metadata	Secret field
TruffleHog (unverified on)	2 Postgres URLs	no	—
ProwlBench (24,603 cases, independent)

Same protocol as Lercas/prowlbench. Gitleaks and TruffleHog match the published leaderboard, so the row is comparable. Prowl cascade is quoted, not re-run.

Cite this table as SecSentry 1.2.0 only (source commit 8c96549; artifact eval/results/prowlbench_leaderboard.json, 2026-09-04). There is no v1.2.0 git tag. Later versions (1.3.0, 1.3.1, 1.4.0) changed detectors; they are a different binary and must not be reported against these figures until the harness is re-run.

Tool	Precision	Recall	F1
Prowl cascade (published)	0.951	0.823	0.883
Gitleaks	0.931	0.413	0.573
SecSentry 1.2.0	0.951	0.347	0.509
TruffleHog	0.940	0.303	0.458
Highest precision of the three we ran. T1 structured-token recall is 0.64 vs Gitleaks 0.65. Overall recall is 0.347 vs 0.413 because T2 generic-context is 0.01 vs 0.35. Rebuild with python -m secsentry.eval.build_corpus && python -m secsentry.eval.benchmark.

Tool	Precision	Recall	F1
SecSentry 1.2.0	1.00	1.00	1.00
Gitleaks 8.30.1	1.00	0.76	0.86
TruffleHog 3.97.4	1.00	0.40	0.57

Scan for SQL injection, XSS, or vulnerable dependencies.
Detect secrets in binaries, or anything deliberately obfuscated.

secsentry scan . --history                # every commit
secsentry scan --staged                   # index only
secsentry scan . --severity high          # filter by severity
secsentry scan . --type aws --type github # filter by detector

secsentry scan . --format html -o report.html
secsentry scan . --format sarif -o secsentry.sarif
secsentry serve . --history               # dashboard, loopback only

secsentry uninstall-hook

File	Purpose

- uses: umeraamir69/secsentry@v1.0.0

    fail-on: high

go build -o secsentry ./cmd/secsentry

python3 scripts/check_version_sync.py
VERSION, internal/version/version.go, and packages/npm/package.json must always agree; CI enforces it.

Layout

cmd/secsentry/        CLI entry point
internal/
├── detect/           regex rules, keyword prefilter, Shannon entropy
├── verify/           local structural checks, no network
├── classify/         heuristics + local BPE rarity
├── scan/             engine, decode, archives, history, aggregate, ignore
├── gitutil/          subprocess git, unique blob walk

notes/                Obsidian vault: plan, ADRs, runbooks
There is one detector implementation. The npm package, the GitHub Action, and any future web UI all shell out to the Go binary rather than reimplementing it.

Architecture decisions

The reasoning behind the non-obvious choices lives in notes/decisions/: git via subprocess rather than a library, history via blob dedup, masking rules, localhost-only dashboard, one engine across two registries, and no live verification.

License

MIT. Every credential in the tests, the demo repo, and the eval corpus is fake.

I spent years pip install-ing and npm install-ing other people's packages. This is the first time I shipped one of my own.

SecSentry — a Git incident scanner for leaked secrets. v1.4.0 is live on GitHub, PyPI, and npm.

The problem:
Vibe coding made it easy to paste a key and git push. Gitleaks and TruffleHog already exist. You delete the key, the tree looks clean, and it’s still in git log  and once that commit exists, a push puts it on GitHub. Most tools either miss that incident, reprint the secret, or send it to a vendor to “verify.”

What I built:
secsentry scan . --history walks every commit, reads each unique blob once, and reports what leaked, where, who introduced it, whether it’s still in HEAD, and how to rotate it. Values are always masked  nothing sent to a vendor API. A pre-commit hook blocks the commit if a key is staged, so it never reaches GitHub in the first place.

On my public demo repo, I committed fake keys, then deleted them:
→ Working tree: 0 findings
→ Full history: 8 unique secrets, 11 occurrences — all flagged as deleted from HEAD, still in history

There's also a localhost dashboard, JSON/HTML/SARIF output, a pre-commit hook, and a GitHub Action that comments on PRs.

Not claiming this replaces Gitleaks or TruffleHog. I benchmarked against both  ahead on precision, behind on recall for unstructured secrets and wrote up why, instead of cherry-picking the numbers that flatter it.
